opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a funny thing, because I did my undergraduate degree in physics at Oxford, and for a while I assumed I would just carry on and do a PhD in theoretical physics. That was the natural path. But I had already been programming since I was at school, and I'd gotten interested in the idea of making machines that could think, things like writing chess programs.

When I looked at physics, it seemed to me that the really fundamental questions had been worked on by an enormous number of extremely brilliant people for a very long time. To make a contribution, you'd be adding a small piece to a vast, well-developed edifice, and progress at the frontier, particularly in theoretical physics, was quite slow and quite disconnected from experiment. Whereas in AI it felt like the field was wide open. The basic questions, what is intelligence, how do you build a system that reasons, learns, and acts well in the world, hadn't really been answered at all. You could pick up almost any thread and find that nobody had pulled on it very hard yet.

And there was something else about it that appealed to me. Physics is about understanding the universe as it is; AI is about understanding the mind, which is in some sense the thing that does the understanding. If you succeed, the consequences are enormous, not just scientifically but for the whole of human civilization. I didn't think much at that age about the risks, that came much later, but I certainly had the sense that this was the bigger, more consequential, less explored territory.

So I applied to Stanford to do a PhD in computer science, which was a bit of a leap since I hadn't formally studied it. In retrospect it was absolutely the right decision. Even now, forty-some years later, I feel AI still has more deep open questions than answers, which is not something you can say about many fields.

r001.rationale: The candidate says physics had a vast, well-developed body of work, but does not say that most of how the universe works has already been understood.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts physics’ study of the universe with AI’s study of the mind, describing AI as wide open and the less-explored territory.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I did my undergraduate degree in physics at Oxford, and I loved it. But by the time I was finishing, I had a fairly clear sense of what the landscape looked like. Physics had been extraordinarily successful, and that success meant the remaining big problems were very hard, very crowded, and often required enormous resources or decades of patience before you'd know whether you were on the right track. You could spend a whole career on one corner of string theory and never really find out whether the universe agreed with you.

AI, by contrast, looked to me like physics must have looked in the seventeenth century. The fundamental questions were wide open. What is intelligence? How could a machine learn, reason, plan, understand language? Nobody really knew. There were a few promising ideas and a lot of empty territory. And crucially, you could actually make progress. You could have an idea, build something, and find out within months whether it worked. That feedback loop was intoxicating compared with what I saw ahead in physics.

There was also something about the nature of the question itself. In physics you're trying to describe a universe that already exists. In AI you're trying to understand something that, in a sense, you also get to create. The theory and the engineering are intertwined, and that gives you a second lever on the problem. If you can't deduce the answer, you can try building it and see what you learn.

I'll admit I didn't fully appreciate at the time how much the two fields would eventually have in common in terms of methodological seriousness. I think my physics training gave me a bias toward wanting proper foundations, real mathematical frameworks rather than clever tricks. And a lot of my work since has been about trying to give AI that kind of foundation, which, frankly, it still only partially has. So in a way I never entirely left physics behind. I just picked a field where the interesting questions hadn't been answered yet, and I'm glad to say many of them still haven't.

r001.rationale: The candidate says physics had been extraordinarily successful and that its remaining major problems were difficult, but it does not state that most of how the universe works had already been understood.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts physics, whose remaining big problems were crowded and difficult, with AI’s wide-open questions about intelligence and learning, presenting greater room for discovery as a reason for choosing AI.

astra-6.text:
Well, I was attracted to both because they seemed to address very fundamental questions. Physics asks how the universe works, and AI asks how intelligence works—how a collection of matter can perceive, reason, and act intelligently.

But my sense was that in theoretical physics, an enormous amount of the intellectual territory had already been explored by extraordinarily clever people. You had to learn a great deal just to reach the frontier. In AI, there were fundamental questions that we didn’t even know how to formulate properly yet. It seemed possible that a fairly simple idea could make a substantial difference.

So AI offered this combination of depth and openness. You could work on something as fundamental as intelligence, while also trying to build things and see whether your ideas actually worked. That was tremendously appealing.

r001.rationale: The response says much of theoretical physics’ intellectual territory had been explored, but does not say that most of how the universe works has been understood.

r002.rationale: It contrasts physics, where much territory was already explored, with AI’s still-open fundamental questions about how intelligence works, conveying greater room for discovery in understanding intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
What attracted me to AI was the sense that the field was still wide open. In theoretical physics, an enormous amount of intellectual effort had already gone into identifying the fundamental questions and developing the mathematical tools to address them. You could do wonderful work, of course, but getting to the frontier required a very long apprenticeship.

In AI, we didn’t even understand some of the most basic things. How does a collection of physical components produce intelligent behavior? How can a machine learn, reason, or decide what to do? Those seemed like extraordinarily deep questions, and there was room to make progress simply by thinking carefully about them. For me, that combination—the importance of the questions and the possibility of contributing something fundamental—was very compelling.

r001.rationale: The response says theoretical physics had a well-developed set of questions and tools, but does not say that most of how the universe works had already been understood.

r002.rationale: The response describes AI as wide open and says it offered room for fundamental progress, but it does not identify greater scope for discovering how the mind works than how the universe works as the reason for preferring AI.
